paragraphs.source_en: When the drier climate prevailed life was probably difficult but nevertheless still possible. The capacity of humans and animals to adapt to extremely arid conditions is confirmed by the ethnographic record from Southern Africa. Hunter-gatherers are able to survive in the desert with the minimum of resources by adopting a large spectrum of strategies, including periodically moving in search of food and water (Silberbauer 1965; Lee 1979). Even today many species of wild animal live in the Sahara as well as nomadic groups with their domesticated goats. Although we have no direct evidence of the human occupation of the Central Sahara before 10,000 BP, there is evidence of human population in the North and Sub-Saharan Africa and Egypt from this period (Aumassip 1986; Sutton 1977; Tillet 1997; Barich 1998a).

paragraphs.source_en: In the generally arid period between 20,000 and 15,600 BP the Central Saharan mountains may have been populated by small groups of huntergatherers, who survived by hunting small animals as well as the only larger animals able to survive in harsh climate, antelope and mouflon. The coexistence of people with antelope and mouflon during arid phases may have created a relationship between the hunter-gatherers and these quadrupeds which penetrated into their ideology, beliefs and spiritual world. This may explain why antelope and mouflon had the privileged position in the paintings and this privilege would continue also during the humid phase, when other large animals populated the region.

paragraphs.source_en: So, when did people start to depict these animals and themselves? Although there was the onset of precipitation in the Acacus at 15,600 BP the surrounding lowlands remained dry (Cremaschi & Di Lernia 1996a). The lakes in Murzuq next to the Acacus did not form before 10,000 BP which suggests that humans and animals could only live in the mountainous zone. When the wettest period ended in the mountains at around 9,700 BP, the precipitation occurred in the lowlands and lakes formed across the whole Central Saharan region (Hachid 1998; Jelinek 2004). In this period large wild African fauna would have spread across the previously dry lowlands to the mountains, following the rivers from the mountains down into the Southern Sahara.
